la:noun:procurator.html:
prōcūrātor (the first
o short, ), ōris, m.
procuro
, a manager, overseer, superintendent, agent, administrator, deputy, procurator, keeper.
In gen. (class.): procurator peni,: procurator, alieni juris vicarius,: agere aliquid per procuratorem, (15): regni,a viceroy,: curatori aquarum procuratorem subicit,: aviarii,: procurator nimium procurat,: esse procuratorem in rem alicujus,: procuratorem facere,.—
In partic.
A manager of an estate, a steward, bailiff (class.; cf. villicus),: procurator rationes accipiebat,; ; .—
In the time of the emperors, one who had charge of the imperial revenues, an imperial collector, ; ; ; ; .—Esp., in a province: Judeae,: Asiae,: Aegypti,: Galliae,; or in a city: urbis,: ludi,.—
An agent or attorney to conduct an action at law, ; ; .

senses: to show oneself, appear, become visible
to go towards, go to meet
to arrive at a certain result, turn out, succeed
la:verb:procedo.html:
prō-cēdo, cessi, cessum, 3, v. n.,
to go forth or before, to go forwards, advance, proceed (class.; cf.: progredior, prodeo).
Lit.
In gen.: procedere ad forum,: illuc procede,: a portu,: ante agmen, : nil cum procede re lintrem Sentimus,: pedibus aequis,: passu tacito,.—
In partic.
In milit. lang., to go or march forwards, to advance, : lente atque paulatim proceditur,; : agmen procedit,; : processum in aciem est,: ipsi jam pridem avidi certaminis procedunt,.—Cf. of ships, ; .—
Of processions, to go on, set forward, move on, advance, etc.: funus interim Procedit: sequimur,; : tacito procedens agmine,: vidisti Latios consul procedere fasces,.—
Transf.
To go or come forth or out, to advance, issue: foribus foras procedere,: castris,: extra munitiones,: in medium,: e tabernaculo in solem,: in pedes procedere nascentem, contra naturam est,to be born feet first,: mediā procedit ab aulā,.—
In gen., to show one's self, to appear: cum veste purpureā procedere,: obviam alicui procedere,to go towards, go to meet,; cf.: Jugurthae obvius procedit,: obviam,: procedat vel Numa,.—
In partic., to issue from the mouth, to be uttered: sed interdum voces procedebant contumaces et inconsultae,; .—
Of stars, etc., to rise, come into view: Ecce Dionaei processit Caesaris astrum,: vesper,.—
Of the moon, to wax, increase, .—
Of plants, to put forth, spring forth, grow (ante-class. and in post-Aug. prose): antequam radices longius procedere possint,: plerumque germen de cicatrice procedit,: gemma sine dubio processura,; et saep.—
Of place, to project, extend: ita ut in pedes binos fossa procedat,: Lydia super Ioniam procedit,: promuntorium, quod contra Peloponnesum procedit,; .—
Trop.
Of time, to advance, pass, elapse (class.): ubi plerumque noctis processit,; : jamque dies alterque dies processit,: dies procedens,: procedente tempore,in process of time,: si aetate processerit,: tempus processit,: procedente die,; : procedunt tempora tarde,: incipient magni procedere menses,: pars major anni jam processerat,.—
To come or go forth, to appear, to present or show one's self (poet. and post-Aug.): nunc volo subducto gravior procedere voltu,i. e. to conduct myself more gravely, to undertake more serious matters, (3, 1), 9: quis postea ad summam Thucydidis, quis Hyperidis ad famam processit?.—
In partic., to go or get on, to advance, make progress (class.; cf. proficio): dicendi laude multum,: in philosophiā,: honoribus longius,; cf. : ad virtutis aditum,: ambitio et procedendi libido,a passion for getting on, for rising in the world,: longius iras,: perspicuum est, quo compositiones unguentorum processerint,to what extent, how far,: ut ratione et viā procedat oratio,: eo vecordiae processit, ut,went so far in folly,: Adherbal, ubi intellegit eo processum,; so, processit in id furoris,: eoque ira processit, ut, etc.,: ex infimā fortunā in ordinem senatorium, et ad summos honores,.—
To run on, continue, remain: et cum stationes procederent, prope obruentibus infirmum corpus armis,i. e. guard duty returned so frequently as to seem continuous,: ut iis stipendia procederent,; ; cf. aera,.—
To go on, continue, follow; esp. of speech, etc.: ad dissuadendum,; cf. : non imitor λακωνισμὸν tuum: altera jam pagella procedit,.—
To

turn out, result, succeed, prosper (class.): parum procedere,; ; : nonnumquam summis oratoribus non satis ex sententiā eventum dicendi procedere,: alicui pulcherrime,: alicui bene,: omnia prospere procedent,.—Impers. (cf. succedo): quibus cum parum procederet, Cael. ap. ; cf.: velut processisset Spurio Licinio,.—Absol., to turn out or succeed well: mane quod tu occoeperis negotium agere, id totum procedit diem,: ferme ut quisque quidque occoeperit, sic ei procedunt post principia,: Syre, processisti hodie pulcre,have succeeded finely,: si processit,: quod si consilia Andranodoro processissent,.—

To turn out favorably for, to result in favor of, to benefit, be of use to one: totidem dies emptori procedent,: benefacta mea reipublicae procedunt,; .—
To be effectual: venenum non processerat,: medicina processit,.—
To go or pass for, to be counted or reckoned as any thing (anteand post-class.): ut binae (oves) pro singulis procedant,shall be reckoned as one,; : quod ita procedit, si ea, cui donabatur, eum interposuit,.—
To happen, take place, occur (ante-class.): numquid processit ad forum hodie novi?.—
To come or proceed from, to be derived from (post-class.): res, quae a sacratissimis imperatoribus procedunt,.— In part. pass.: in processā aetate,advanced,.

la:noun:procuratio.html:
prōcūrātĭo, ōnis, f.
procuro
.
In gen.
A caring for, taking care of, having the charge of a thing; a charge, superintendence, administration, management, procuration (class.): dum me rei publicae non solum cura, sed quaedam etiam procuratio multis officiis implicatum et constrictum tenebat,: dum necesse erat, unus omnia poterat: qui, postea quam magistratus creavit, sua cuique procuratio auctoritasque est restituta,: procuratio templi,: mearum rerum existimationisque meae,: rerum humanarum,: ministerii,: annonae,: male gesta,.—In plur.: ad amplissimas procurationes promotus,charges, offices,.—
An effort, aim, seeking for any thing (post-class.): quia benignitas eum per sese ipsa delectet, sine ullā recipiendae gratiae procuratione,.—
In partic., of religious acts, an averting or expiating of an evil omen or crime by offering the proper sacrifices, an expiatory sacrifice, expiation (class.): cum terrae motus factus esset, ut sue plena procuratio fieret,: prodigii,: procurationes incesti,.

la:noun:procella.html:
prŏcella, ae,
f [pro and root kel; Gr. κέλης, runner; cf.: celer, celox], a violent wind (by which things are prostrated), a storm, hurricane, tempest (class.).
Lit.: procella distat latitudine a vortice et a turbine disjectā nube verius quam ruptā,: turbinis inmanem vim provomit atque procellae,: imbres, nimbi, procellae, turbines,; : creber procellis Africus,: stridens Aquilone procella,: si mugiat Africis Malus procellis,; : praecipites,: navis quassata procellā,: raperent mea poma procellae, id. Nux, 163: procella nivem effuderat,: imbrem excusserant procellae,: Thalle, turbidā rapacior procellā,.—With gen.: validi venti collecta procella,.—
Transf.
(Mostly in plur.) A storm, tumult, violence, commotion, vehemence: tempestates et procellas in illis fluctibus concionum, (also cited ap. , and particularly mentioned as a figure, ): vita tranquilla et quieta remota a procellis invidiarum,: ut procellam temporis devitaret,: patriae,: agitari tribuniciis procellis,; cf.: seditionum procellae,: procellae civiles,civil commotions,; cf.: ferimur procellā,; .—
In milit. lang.
A charge, onset, sudden attack of cavalry: hac velut procellā ita consternavit equos, ut, etc.,: equestrem procellam excitemus oportet,: equestris,; .—
In gen., of a fierce battle: hic secunda belli Punici procella desaevit,; .—
Of a storm of eloquence: priusquam illam eloquentiae procellam effunderet (Ulixes),: contionum,.

la:verb:procello.html:
prō-cello, ĕre, v. a.
cf.: percello, procella, celer
,
to throw or cast down (anteclass.): procello, περιτρέπω, Gloss. Philox.: procellunt sese in mensam, i. e. lie down (at table), Ritschl N. cr.; cf.: procellunt, procumbunt, Paul. ex Müll.

la:adv:procul.html:
prŏcul, adv.
procello, to drive away
,
in the distance, at a distance, a great way off, far, afar off, from afar.
Lit., of place (class.; cf.: longe, eminus); constr. absol.; with adv. of place; with ab and abl. (not in Cic., Cæs., or Sall.); with abl. alone: cuja vox sonat procul?: sequi procul,: non jam procul, sed hic praesentes sua templa dii defendunt,. 29: ubi turrim constitui procul viderunt,: jubet, ut procul tela coniciant, neu propius accedant,: procul attendere,: procul e fluctu Trinacria,: est procul in pelago saxum,: procul et e longinquo,: omnibus arbitris procul amotis,: procul o, procul este, profani,keep aloof!: cui procul astanti, Pettalus irridens dixit,; cf.: adstans non procul,.—With other particles of place, as hinc, inde, alicunde, longe, etc.: procul hinc stans,at a distance from this place,; : istic procul,: istinc procul,: procul inde,: procul alicunde,: procul longe,.— With a or ab, far from, far away from (class.): procul a terrā abripi,: esse procul a conspectu,far out of sight,: a castris,: a portā,: ab Ariciā,: ab hoste,: a domo,; : a patriā,; : a mari,: a Pado,: a litore,: ab ore,: a fratre,: a mari,—With simple abl., far from, far away from: patriā procul, Enn. ap. (Trag. v. 295 Vahl.): urbe,: ripā Tiberis,: oppido,: moenibus,: Nomento,: mari,: haud procul castris,: Teutoburgiensi Saltu,: regno,: non procul Euripidis poëtae sepulcro,: urbe Romā,: oppido,.—
Trop., far, distant, remote; constr, with ab, the abl., or absol.: conscia mihi sum a me culpam hanc esse procul,: procul ab omni metu,: viri, qui sunt procul ab aetatis hujus memoriā,: caelestia procul sunt a nostrā cognitione,: res procul ab ostentatione positae,: quis tam procul a litteris, quin sic incipiat,so unacquainted with letters, so unlettered,; : ab odio, ab irā,: a sapiente,: ab omni negotio,: a praesenti modestiā,.— With simple abl.: liber invidiā, procul contentionibus,: eam (plebem) procul urbe haberi,out of public affairs,: procul negotiis,: ambitione,: voluptatibus habere aliquem,to keep one aloof from enjoyments, deprive him of them,: tali more,: procul dubio,without doubt,; ; ; ; ; for which: dubio procul,; : procul vero est,far from the truth, untrue,fin.—Absol.: assentatio vitiorum adjutrix procul amoveatur,: homines superbissimi procul errant,err widely, greatly,: pauperies immunda domus procul absit, i.e. pauperies domestica procul absit,: durabisne procul dominoque legere superstes, Thebai?: non procul est quin, it does not want much of, etc., almost, nearly, : haud procul est quin Romam agnosceret,.—
In partic. (post-Aug. and very rare), in estimation of value, far removed from, much inferior to: aes suo colore pretiosum, procul a Corinthio (est), is far beneath or inferior to, much poorer than, .

la:adj:procax.gloss: bold, brash, shameless, impudent, insolent, forward, pert, saucy, wanton
senses: bold, brash, shameless, impudent, insolent, forward, pert, saucy, wanton
la:adj:procax.html:
prŏcax, ācis, adj.
id.
,
bold, shameless, impudent, insolent, forward, pert, wanton (class.; syn.: petulans, protervus).
Of persons: leno procax, rapax, trahax,: procaciores estis vos,: non solum meretrix, sed etiam procax,: procax in lacessendo,: procax ore,: ingenio,: lingua,: moribus,.—With gen.: procax otii, i. e. in otio,. —
Of things: procaces manus,: Fescennina locutio,: sermo,: libertas,: nequitiae procaciores,: aliquem procacibus scriptis diffamare,: procacissima lixarum ingenia,: mulier meretrix et procax,.—Of the vine: maritas populos complexae, atque per ramos earum procacibus brachiis scandentes, with wanton arms, i. e. entwining tendrils, .—Poet.: Auster,i. e. stormy,.—Hence, adv.: prŏcācĭter, boldly, impudently, wantonly (not in Cic. or Cæs.): finem procaciter orto sermoni imponere,: procacius stipendium flagitare quam ex modestiā militari. ; : procacissime patris tui memoriam illudunt,: vultum obfirmare,.

la:noun:procer.html:
prŏcer, ĕris, in sing. only , and ; prŏcĕres, um (anteclass. collat. form prŏcus, i, in the
gen. plur.: procum patricium in descriptione classium quam facit, Serv. Tullius, significat procerum, Müll.; cf.: jam (ut censoriae tabulae loquuntur) fabrum et procum audeo dicere, non fabrorum et procorum,), m.
pro and root kar- of creo; cf. procērus
.
Lit., a chief, noble; plur., the leading men, chiefs, nobles, princes (class.; syn.: primores, optimates, primi): scindunt proceres Pergamum, the Grecian chiefs, princes, * : audiebam nostros proceres clamitantes,: Latinorum,: Etruscorum,: ego proceribus civitatis annumeror,: Caecina Largus e proceribus,: delectos populi ad proceres,: castrorum,: in procerum coetu,; ; : proceres rerum,.—Transf., of bees: procerum seditio,.—In sing.: agnosco procerem,: in pueritiā fuit pastor nonnumquam et procer,a leader, captain,.—
Trop., the foremost or most celebrated men, the masters in an art, science, etc. (post-Aug.): proceres artis ejus (medicinae),: sapientiae,: gulae,: indicatis in genere utroque (pingendi) proceribus,.

la:verb:procumbo.html:
prō-cumbo, cŭbŭi, cŭbĭtum, 3, v. n.
Lit., to fall forwards, fall or sink down, to prostrate one's self; of the wounded, the dying, suppliants, etc. (class.; cf.; cado, ruo): procumbunt Gallis omnibus ad pedes Bituriges, ne pulcherrimam urbem succendere cogerentur,: genibus, Ov M. 13, 585: ad genua alicujus, Liv 25, 7: ad pedes alicujus,: ante pedes,; : templis, (1, 2, 83): qui vulneribus confecti procubuissent,; so, in genua,: Coroebus Penelei dextrā Procumbit,.—With dat. (post-Aug.): sibi tres legiones procubuisse,had yielded,: veteranae cohortes, quibus nuper Othonis legiones procubuerint,.—Poet., to fall upon, attack, .—To lean or bend forwards: olli certamine summo Procumbunt,i.e. they bend to their oars,.—
Transf., of inanimate subjects, to lean forwards, bend down, sink, to be beaten or broken down (class.): tigna prona ac fastigiata, ut secundum naturam fluminis procumberent,: frumenta imbribus procubuerant,i.e. were beaten down,: ne gravidis procumbat culmus aristis,: ulmus in aram ipsam procumbebat,.— Of buildings: (domus) in domini procubuit caput,: tecta super habitantes,; ; .—
To be upset, break down; of a vehicle: nam si procubuit qui saxa Ligustica portat Axis, Juv 3, 257.—
Trop., to fall or sink down (poet. and post-Aug.): procumbere in voluptates, to sink into sen

suality, : procumbentem rem publicam restituere,sinking,: res procubuere meae,.—

To extend, spread: mons Haemus vasto jugo procumbens in Pontum,: planities sub radicibus montium spatiosa procumbit,.

la:verb:proclamo.gloss: to call or cry out, vociferate; proclaim, declare
senses: to call or cry out, vociferate; proclaim, declare
la:verb:proclamo.html:
pro-clāmo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a.,
to call or cry out, to vociferate.
In gen. (class.): assunt, defendunt, proclamant,: patre proclamante, se filiam jure caesam judicare,: magnā proclamat voce Diores,: quid non proclames, si, etc., .—
In partic., in jurid. lang.
To defend, to clamor in defence: proclamando pro sordidis hominibus, (cf. proclamator).—
Proclamare ad or in libertatem, to assert one's liberty, to appeal to the judge to maintain one's liberty: ad libertatem,; ; cf.: ad ingenuitatem,: in libertatem,; .

la:verb:procurvo.html:
prō-curvo, āre, 1, v. a.,
to bend or curve forwards (poet.): aliquem,: pomiferique simul procurvant bracchia rami, Auct. Carm. de Genesi, 14.

la:verb:proco.html:
prŏco, āre, v. a., and prŏcor, āri, v. dep.
cf. precor
,
to ask, demand (very rare): parere mea vos majestas procat, Liv. And. ap. : a procando, id est poscendo, procacitas nominata est, (ap. ): procare, poscere, unde procaces meretrices ab assidue poscendo, et proci uxorem poscentes in matrimonium, Paul. ex Müll.: poscere procare dictum, ib.: perit, inquit, procari, si latet,, praef. 5.
la:verb:proco.inflection: āre, v. a., āri, v. dep.

la:other:Procas.gloss: A mythological king of Alba Longa, father of Numitor, great-grandfather of Romulus and Remus
senses: A mythological king of Alba Longa, father of Numitor, great-grandfather of Romulus and Remus
la:other:Procas.html:
Prŏcas and Prŏca, ae, m.,
a king of Alba: Proca Numitorem atque Amulium procreat,; ; ; : proximus ille Procas,.

senses: to take care of, attend to, look after any thing
la:verb:procuro.html:
prō-cūro (the first
o scanned short, ; ), āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. and n., to take care of, attend to, look after any thing.
In gen. (class.; syn.: curam gero).
Act.: nunc tu te interim, quasi pro puerperā, hic procuras,: pueros,; cf.: nunc puero utere et procura,: hic sunt trecenti nummi ... hinc me procura,: corpora,: sacrificia,: sacra,: arbores,: semina,: plantas,.—
Neutr., with dat., to look after, care for (ante- and post-class.): bene procuras mihi,: victui potuique,.—
In partic., to take care of, to manage one's affairs (class.).
Act.: procurat negotia Dionysii,: hereditatem,.—Hence, of religious acts, to avert or expiate (evil omens) by sacrifice (cf.: expio, lustro): monstra,: procurare atque expiare signa, quae a diis hominibus portenduntur,; ; ; : ostentum,: fulgur,: sacrificio ostentorum ac fulgurum denuntiationes procurantur,.—
Neutr., to hold a charge or administration, to be procurator: cum procuraret in Hispaniā,: procurante Pontio Pilato Judaeam,; .—With dat. of person (post-class.): procurare patri,to act as agent for,; .— With dat. of thing: operibus publicis,.—Of religious acts, to make expiation or atonement: VT CONSVL HOSTIIS MAIORIBVS IOVI ET MARTI PROCVRARET, S. C. ap. .—With ne: ipse procuravi, ne possent saeva nocere Somnia, ter sancta deveneranda mola,.—Impers. pass.: simul procuratum est, quod tripedem mulum Reate natum nuntiatum erat,.
la:verb:procuro.inflection: āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. and n.

la:verb:procurro.html:
prō-curro, cŭcurri and curri, cursum, 3, v. n.,
to run forth, rush forwards.
Lit. (class.), freq. of armies: si Romani ferocius procucurrissent,: infestis pilis,: in proximum tumulum, 39: ad repellendum, et prosequendum hostem,: longius,to rush farther on,: adversos telum contorsit in hostes Procurrens,.—Of animals: qui et procurrentem (bovem) retrahat et cunctantem producat,; .—
Transf.
Of locality, to run or jut out, to extend, project (poet. and in post-Aug. prose): infelix saxis in procurrentibus haesit,: terra procurrit in aequor,: mons procurrit in occidentem,: procurrens per medium Euxinum promontorium,: Clupea procurrit a Punico litore,; ; .—
Of plants, to extend: radix in longitudinem procurrens,.—
Of money, to increase: in ipso procurrentis pecuniae impetu raptus,.— *
Trop., to go on, advance: ut productus studio, ultra facile procurras,that you may advance beyond it,.
la:verb:procurro.inflection: cŭcurri and curri, cursum, 3, v. n.

la:other:Prochyta.html:
Prŏchўta, ae, and Prŏchўtē, ēs, f., = Προχύτη,
a small Italian island near Campania, the mod. Procida, ; ; ; ; ; .

la:adj:procerus.html:
prōcērus, a, um, adj.
pro and root karof creo; cf. Gr. κράτος, κρατερός
,
high, tall, long.
Lit. (class.; cf. excelsus): procerum collum,: boves cornibus proceris,: in procero corpore,: homo procerae staturae,: habitu procerus,: pueritia,: homo procerior,: usus est calceamentis altiusculis, ut procerior videretur,: (Galatea) floridior pratis, longa procerior alno,: inter hos procerissimos populos,: procerissimus quisque,: cohortes,: statura,.—Of plants, trees: procerissimae populi,: quid enim abiete procerius?: proceras lauros,: silvae,; : Pompeianum (genus) procerius,.—
In partic., perh. the name of a company of tall soldiers, similar to our grenadiers: VETERANVS EX PROCERIORIBVS,.—
Transf., in gen., long, extended, large: passus,: aves procero rostro, Cic. N. D. 1, 36, 101: lupi,large,; cf.: thoes, luporum id genus est, procerius longitudine,: procerior cauda,: dextera,: proceriores uniones,: cucurbitae,: syllabae procerae sunt, quae vocalem longam habent in paenultima, ut facultas, long, Varr. ap. P.: anapaestus, procerior numerus,.— Poet.: plangebant aliae proceris tympana palmis,i. e. outstretched, upraised,.—Hence, * adv.: prōcērē; comp.: bracchium procerius projectum,stretched out to a greater length,.

la:verb:proculco#2.html:
prō-culco, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a.
calco
,
to tread down, trample upon (mostly poet. and in post-Aug. prose).
Lit.: turbatus eques sua ipse subsidia territis equis proculcavit,: crescenti segetes proculcat in herbā,; cf. Sev. ap. —Of a Centaur: pedibusque virum proculcat equinis,: solum,: uvas,; cf. ; : nepotem,trample to death,: una ala ipso impetu proculcata erat,crushed,: aliquem,: materiam,: qui tot proculcavimus nives, have trodden, i. e. traversed, .—
Trop., to trample upon, tread under foot, despise: qui fata proculcavit,: proculcato senatu,: proculcata desertaque respublica,: contumeliosā voce,.—Hence, prōculcātus, a, um, P. a., trodden down; trop., = tritus, trodden under foot, mean, low, common (post-class.): verba proculcata vulgo et protrita,; cf. .

la:adj:proclivis.html:
prōclīvis, e (ante- and post-class. and poet.; collat. form prōclīvus, a, um, ; ; ; ; v. Neue, Formenl. 2, p. 91), adj.
proclivus
,
sloping, steep, going downwards or downhill.
Lit. (rare; not in Cic. or Cæs.: solum,: per proclivem viam duci,: omnia procliva sunt; facile descenditur,.—Subst.: prō-clīve, is (or prōclīvum, i), n., a slope, descent, declivity: pelli per proclive,downhill, downwards,: adjuvante proclivo impetum militum, (al. proclivio): in proclive detrudi, Auct. B. Alex. 76: per proclivia devolare,.—Of persons, going downwards or downhill (poet.), .—
Trop.
Downwards, descending, downhill, declining (rare but class.): proclivi cursu et facili delabi,: jam proclivi senectute,declining, drawing to a close,; cf.: Junius mensis est jam proclivus in Julium,.—Absol.: proclivi currit oratio,flows precipitately,; v. Madv. ad h. l.—
Inclined or disposed to a thing, liable, prone, subject; ready, willing (freq. and class.; mostly in a bad sense; cf. , s. v. proclivitas; syn. propensus); constr. usually ad aliquid, more rarely with dat. or circa.
With ad: ingenium Hominum proclive ad lubidinem,: ad aliquem morbum proclivior,: ergo et invidi et malevoli...quia proclives ad eas perturbationes,: amicitia debet esse ad omnem comitatem facilitatemque proclivior,.—
With dat. (poet.): sceleri proclivis egestas,.—
With circa (post-Aug.): eritque judex circa modestiam juris probatione proclivior,.—
Steep, unsafe, untrustworthy; and hence, obscure, unintelligible: fecisti modo mi ex proclivo planum,you make it plain,: faciam hanc rem planam ex proclivā tibi,: nam iste proclive'st quod jubes me plane conlocare,.—
Transf., easy to be done: proclivia anteponuntur laboriosis,: illa facilia, proclivia, jucunda,: ut fingendi proclivis esset ratio,: proclivus impetus,: cum proclivior faciliorque jactus sit ex supernis in infima,: dictu quidem est proclive,easy to be said,: quod est multo proclivius,much easier,.— Absol.: in proclivi, easy: tam hoc quidem tibi in proclivi, quam imber est, quando pluit,as easy,: id. faciam, in proclivi quod est,: alia omnia in proclivi erunt,will be easy,; v. planum.—Hence, adv., in two forms, prōclīvē and prō-clīvĭter (cf. ; ).
Downwards: proclive labuntur,rush downwards, Kühn. and Moser N. cr. (B. and K. proclivi); Lachm.; cf. sublime ferri, under sublimis.—Comp.: labi verba proclivius,i. e. more rapidly,; cf.: quin proclivius hic iras decurrat ad acris,.—
Easily: facile et procliviter persuadere, Castric. ap. .—Comp.: multo proclivius,.
